clue.text: Lay out a thousand on crucial employment to discover sharp practice

parts.note: M is the Roman numeral for a thousand
on is taken as written, placed after the thousand
something crucial is key
one's employment is one's business

explanation.surface: A gambler stakes a thousand pounds on a vital job and uncovers dishonest dealing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lay out' reads like spending money, and 'monkey' is British slang for five hundred pounds, which may tempt a wrong count; here it only sets the betting scene, with M, ON, KEY and BUSINESS in a row.
explanation.definitionFit: Sharp practice is underhand or dishonest dealing, the mischief the idiom names.

clue.text: Spoil a little child, and it may go to pot

parts.note: to spoil something is to mar it
a mite is a small child

explanation.surface: Indulge a small child too much and it will be ruined.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Go to pot' sounds like ruin, continuing the spoiling picture, but the definition is literal: Marmite is a British yeast spread sold in a pot, and marmite is also French for a cooking pot.
explanation.definitionFit: The yeast extract is sold in a squat jar, so it is something that goes into a pot.

clue.text: Bananas in ancient Rome

parts.note: bananas is slang for crazy; the clue asks for the Latin phrase, the language of ancient Rome, meaning not of sound mind

explanation.surface: A question about whether the Romans ate tropical fruit.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin legal phrase means not in control of one's mind, which is what bananas means in slang.

clue.text: Love proves painful in retrospect

indicators.note: looking back, so the word for painful is read from its end to its start

parts.note: something painful is sore

explanation.surface: Romance turns out to hurt when you look back on it.
explanation.definitionFit: The Greek god of love gives his name to erotic desire.

clue.text: It's twice as good in Paris, sweet

indicators.note: twice says the French word is written two times over

parts.note: bon is French for good

explanation.surface: Things are doubly good in the French capital, which is lovely.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sweet' looks like an adjective praising Paris but is the definition, a noun.
explanation.definitionFit: A bonbon is a small confection, a type of candy.

clue.text: They buy small jumpers

parts.note: S is the usual abbreviation for small, as on clothing labels
hoppers are creatures or people that jump

explanation.surface: Customers purchase little knitted pullovers.
explanation.walkthrough: In British English a jumper is a sweater, which the surface uses; the wordplay wants things that jump.
explanation.definitionFit: Customers in a store are people who buy.

clue.text: Ill health is what the drunk driver is in

definitions.text: what the drunk driver is in

explanation.surface: Poor health compared to the condition of someone driving while intoxicated.
explanation.definitionFit: Being unwell means not fit; a drunk motorist is unfit to drive, both conditions described by the phrase.

clue.text: Subordinate post offered by mediocre daily

parts.note: second-class means inferior or mediocre
the Daily Mail is a British newspaper, so a daily can be the Mail

explanation.surface: A junior job advertised in an undistinguished newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'post' reads as a job, but it means letters; second-class is the cheaper, slower British postal service.
explanation.definitionFit: Second-class mail is the lower tier of postal delivery, post of lesser rank.

clue.text: Blair was otherwise in fine fettle

parts.note: or means otherwise, as in 'hurry, or else'
someone in fine fettle is healthy, well

explanation.surface: A prime minister was in good health in other ways.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blair' suggests Tony Blair, but here it is Eric Blair, the real name of the author of Nineteen Eighty-Four.
explanation.definitionFit: Eric Blair wrote under the pen name George Orwell.

clue.text: Summary reduction in manpower

explanation.surface: A report on staff cuts.
explanation.definitionFit: A rundown is a brief account of the main points, and also a cutting back in staff numbers.

clue.text: One authorised to get the freezer thawed out

parts.note: a freezer switched off thaws out, so off stands for thawed out
an icer is one that ices, a freezer

explanation.surface: Someone with permission defrosting the freezer.
explanation.walkthrough: The charade is in answer order, so the piece for 'thawed out' comes first although it is last in the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: An officer holds a commission, an appointment giving authority to act.

clue.text: Artificial language a fair number regarded with awe?

definitions.note: the definition is a description; the answer is a noun for someone regarded with awe

parts.note: Ido is a constructed language derived from Esperanto
L is the Roman numeral for fifty, a fair number

explanation.surface: A made-up tongue spoken by quite a few, treated with reverence.
explanation.definitionFit: A person or image worshipped or adored is one regarded with awe.

clue.text: Lawful extent of authority necessitates proficiency

explanation.surface: Having legal jurisdiction demands skill.
explanation.definitionFit: Legally the word means the scope of a court's jurisdiction; generally it means skill or ability.

clue.text: More luxurious liner price subject to fluctuation

indicators.note: fluctuating things shift about, so the letters of liner and price are rearranged

explanation.surface: The fare for a better cruise ship varies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'subject to fluctuation' rearranges LINER PRICE into the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Princely means lavish or splendid, so the comparative means more lavish.

clue.text: The adept is no longer disrespectful

parts.note: ex means former, no longer
pert means cheeky or disrespectful

explanation.surface: The skilled person has stopped being cheeky.
explanation.definitionFit: An adept is a skilled person, a master of a field.

clue.text: Etiquette exhibited by the original Blimp

parts.note: proto- means first or original
Colonel Blimp is a British cartoon character, a pompous old officer, so Blimp gives COL, short for Colonel

explanation.surface: Correct manners displayed by a stuffy old military man.
explanation.definitionFit: Protocol is the formal code of conduct and ceremony, especially in diplomacy.

clue.text: Interrupted Edward at home, nonetheless

parts.note: but can mean nevertheless or nonetheless
Ted is a short form of Edward
someone at home is in

explanation.surface: Edward was in all the same, and broke into the conversation.
explanation.walkthrough: The pieces are in answer order: BUT from 'nonetheless' comes first though it ends the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: To butt in is to interrupt a conversation.

clue.text: More than enough water to wash in

explanation.surface: Having an excess of washing water.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I've had a basinful' is a British idiom for having had more than enough of something.
explanation.definitionFit: A bowl filled to the brim holds washing water, and the idiom means a surfeit.

clue.text: Feel cheerier when the dollar's standing high

parts.note: a buck is slang for a dollar
up means raised or high

explanation.surface: Being happier when the currency is strong.
explanation.definitionFit: To buck up is to become more cheerful.

clue.text: Associate with a man of sobriety and a man of honour

parts.note: TT stands for teetotal, someone who never drinks
CH is the Companion of Honour, a British order

explanation.surface: Linking oneself with a sober man and an honourable one.
explanation.walkthrough: CH, Companion of Honour, is a British honour, as are crossword stalwarts like OBE.
explanation.definitionFit: To associate one thing with another is to connect or fasten it to it.

clue.text: Listeners are in the grass, according to rumour

indicators.note: the listening organs are placed inside the word for dried grass

parts.note: hay is dried grass
ears are what we listen with

explanation.surface: People overhearing from the long grass pick up gossip.
explanation.definitionFit: Hearsay is information received from others, unverified talk.

clue.text: Where teachers must present the facts

explanation.surface: Classroom teachers have to give pupils the facts.
explanation.walkthrough: A form is a British school class, so teachers must be in form; the joined word means tell someone the facts.
explanation.definitionFit: Teaching happens in a class, called a form in British schools, and to tell someone facts is to brief them.

clue.text: The fruit that Churchill loved

explanation.surface: Churchill's favourite fruit.
explanation.walkthrough: Churchill's wife was named Clementine, so 'loved' points to his spouse, not a snack.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a small citrus like a mandarin, and was the first name of Winston Churchill's wife.

clue.text: Part of the Burma-Siam landmass

indicators.note: the answer is only a portion of the run of letters in the hyphenated place names

explanation.surface: A region of Southeast Asia around Burma and Siam.
explanation.definitionFit: The continent is the largest landmass on Earth.

clue.text: Look in British Columbia for a powerful alliance

indicators.note: the old exclamation for look goes inside the province's abbreviation

parts.note: BC is the abbreviation for the Canadian province
lo means look, as in 'lo and behold'

explanation.surface: Searching a Canadian province for a strong coalition.
explanation.definitionFit: A bloc is a group of nations or parties united by shared interests.

clue.text: Never tested in court

parts.note: a case or defendant not yet heard by a judge; also anything never put to the test

explanation.surface: A legal case that has never come before a judge.
explanation.definitionFit: A case not yet heard has not been judged, and anything untested has not been tried out.

clue.text: Private lists rescued by the Maid

parts.note: OR, other ranks, means soldiers who are not officers, such as privates
a ship lists or leans to one side

explanation.surface: A soldier's records saved by a housemaid.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the Maid' is Joan of Arc, the Maid of Orleans, who relieved the besieged city in 1429.
explanation.definitionFit: Joan of Arc lifted the English siege of the French city in 1429.

clue.text: A cot is normally battered around enormously

indicators.note: being knocked about scrambles things, so the letters of the four words are rearranged

explanation.surface: A child's bed usually gets badly knocked about.
explanation.walkthrough: 'battered around' rearranges A COT IS NORMALLY.
explanation.definitionFit: Astronomical figures are vast, so the adverb means hugely.
